<reason>Side A won a competitive, high-quality debate. A's core weighing frame — the subsidy's failure is design (pays by fuel burned, cannot reach those who burn none) while every CON objection is implementation, fixable and blameable — structured the late exchange and survived B's best counter ("permanent implementation, renewed forever"). A answered pressure directly: the "remove the top via vehicle and payroll records" move (A4.4) genuinely neutralized B's registry/where-are-the-savings attack, and the "borrow" concession was exploited effectively in the closing. B mounted a genuinely original underdog case (political durability, coalition asymmetry, "fails expensively vs fails silently on the poor") and landed the sharpest single blow with the symmetry argument that cash's rescue vote is no more politically achievable than subsidy abolition. B's sequencing point (transfers funded by savings means prices must rise first) was never squarely answered, but it remained narrow. B also lost more substantive content to clipping (opening, both rebuttals, and closing were truncated), a real execution cost, while A only lost the closing's final sentence. Both sides used plausible background examples without fake precision.</best_rebuttal>
<best_rebuttal>Two exchanges stand out. B2.7's "sequencing is fiscally backwards" went unanswered by A and kept a live route open. But the decisive clash was B's Q2 on where the fiscal savings come from if the program starts near-universal: A's A4.4 answer — targeting by excluding the rich through vehicle and payroll records, converting leakage and the price ceiling into savings delivered to the poor — was the most direct and original neutralization of B's central case, and B's B4.4 pushback ("concedes my point while pretending not to") did not fully erase it.</best_rebuttal>
